transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Quantica CTO), Ben Martin (Quantica ML Eng), Ravi Shah (Quantica Infra)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, good afternoon, thanks for joining. i'm maya from redwood, with diego our systems eng, ready to walk through the edge-case demo.
[00:12] Aisha Patel: hi maya, hey diego, thanks for setting this up. we wanted to see specifically long-context behavior and what happens when we push to high throughput, plus streaming when stuff gets backpressured.
[00:25] Diego Alvarez: great, that's exactly what we planned. quick agenda: 1) long context handling and kv cache behavior; 2) high-TPS routing/auto-scaling; 3) streaming and backpressure/timeouts; 4) Q/A and next steps.
[00:40] Ben Martin: quick note, our production footprint is a mix of on-cloud and some on-prem in EU due to data residency; we'll need VPC options and KMS integration.
[00:50] Maya Chen: totally noted, we'll cover private deployment options and key management.
[01:05] Diego Alvarez: jumping into long context — Redwood supports extended contexts with two main levers: memory-friendly kv caching (sometimes transcripts show as 'KV cash' in our logs ha) and chunked attention pipelines. for example, we've seen customers push 50k to 100k token windows with mixed quantized models. the important bit is the kernel selection and cache eviction policy.
[01:30] Aisha Patel: when you say 100k tokens — what's the latency impact? we care about 95th percentile under 1.2s for our interactive UI.
[01:42] Diego Alvarez: yeah so it depends on model variant and hardware. hosted smaller models with quantization can hit sub-second medians for generate-only flows, but for 100k prefix + 2k generation you're looking at added overhead for cache rehydration. with Dedicated reserved GPUs and tuned kernels we can often keep 95p under 1.5s for batch sizes typical to your UI. we have some tradeoffs — chunking reduces max mem but adds micro-batching latency.
[02:10] Ravi Shah: and memory footprint — do we need more GPUs per slot? we are evaluating unit economics.
[02:18] Diego Alvarez: you'll see higher GPU mem usage with long-kept kv state per session. that's where autoscaling and warm pooling come in; Redwood Dedicated lets you reserve capacity with burst policies to avoid cold-start latencies.
[02:35] Ben Martin: can we snapshot KV state and reuse it across requests? like for multi-step workflows.
[02:42] Diego Alvarez: yes, prefix and KV caching are first-class; we persist session prefix snapshots and can attach them to requests. note the snapshot size and serialization impacts network I/O — we have efficient binary formats but it still matters.
[03:00] Maya Chen: shifting to high TPS — what's your expected TPS numbers and typical request size?
[03:06] Ben Martin: during peak we expect ~2k rps for embeddings and 800 rps for chat/generation; median seq len 700 tokens, 99p ~18k tokens for long reports.
[03:20] Diego Alvarez: OK that's high but within design — routing policy is key. Redwood supports multi-tier routing: cheapest compatible model, latency-first, region-bound, etc. for 2k rps we recommend a mix of hosted for burst and Dedicated for steady-state. autoscaling policies can trigger more instances, but at some point you'll want dedicated pools to hit unit-cost targets.
[03:42] Aisha Patel: what about backpressure — we've seen streaming clients fall over when server throttles. how does Redwood handle streaming backpressure/timeouts?
[03:52] Diego Alvarez: good question. we expose both server-initiated flow control and client-side buffering. streaming is chunked; if downstream consumer can't keep up, the runtime can apply backpressure signals and start buffering up to a configured limit. beyond that, we have graceful degradation: either switch to non-streamed batched response, degrade model variant (faster lower-cost), or drop non-critical tokens. timeouts can be configured per-route with automatic fallback to a cached or summary response.
[04:26] Ben Martin: do you support partial responses and resumable streams? we need our front-end to show progressive results even if network hiccups occur.
[04:34] Diego Alvarez: we do partials, and we can resume from last confirmed token ID if you use the session KV approach. small caveat: resumability is easier on our Dedicated/private deployments where we control the device affinity and cache residency.
[04:50] Ravi Shah: security concerns — KMS, SSO and audit logs. are logs user-level? can we control retention and encryption?
[04:58] Maya Chen: yes, we have per-customer audit logs, retention policies, KMS integration for customer-managed keys in Private deployments; hosted customers get Redwood-managed keys but we offer HSM integrations for enterprise. SOC2 attestation and ISO docs are in the security deck we'll send.
[05:20] Aisha Patel: any known issues with streaming under TLS termination in our load balancer? we run an on-prem LB that sometimes cuts connections after 30s.
[05:28] Diego Alvarez: that's a common gotcha. streaming sessions can be proxied but you have to ensure LB idle timeouts are above your expected longest chunk interval. Redwood Console also shows per-route tail latencies so you can tune keepalive and chunk size.
[05:48] Ben Martin: can you demo a live stream where we simulate a slow consumer and see backpressure behavior?
[05:54] Diego Alvarez: yep — i'll kick off a demo.
[06:00] [DEMO START — screen share noise]
[06:08] Diego Alvarez: starting a synthetic scenario: 1) 10k token context load; 2) concurrent rps to simulate 2k rps; 3) slow client buffer to trigger backpressure.
[06:20] [00:06:20] Diego Alvarez: noticing some chunk delays — runtime is currently buffering up to configured 2MB before applying backpressure policies.
[06:32] Aisha Patel: i see 'buffering' alerts in console, and a fallback triggered — is that switching model variant?
[06:38] Diego Alvarez: yes i configured a fallback chain: primary full-precision long-context model -> quantized long-context -> shorter-context summary model. when buffering crosses threshold we splice to the quantized model to keep throughput.
[06:52] Ben Martin: how do you measure cost when fallback happens — bill by actual tokens generated per variant?
[06:58] Maya Chen: billing is token-level plus model variant rate; when fallback triggers we attribute usage to the variant that served the tokens. Console shows token-level cost breakdown so you can set alerts.
[07:12] Ravi Shah: we want to avoid silent degradation affecting user experience. is there a way to bias routing to prefer latency over cost during peak?
[07:20] Diego Alvarez: yes — routing policies can be set to priority: latency-first for specified routes, and you can set budget gates to fall back only after budget exhausted.
[07:34] Aisha Patel: about timeouts — if the stream doesn't finish in 20s, can we auto-provide a summary instead of a partial hang?
[07:42] Diego Alvarez: absolutely — route-level timeout handler: on timeout send best-effort summary produced from KV or cached result. we also support precomputed summaries to return instantly if SLA violation predicted.
[07:56] Ben Martin: could you run a stress test that measures P95 latency across the whole path including our LB and dark traffic?
[08:04] Diego Alvarez: we can run a benchmark standup. we'll need sample traces and token distribution. diego: action: run sim with both hosted and dedicated to compare economics and P95.
[08:16] Aisha Patel: timeline — we want to pilot within two weeks if the numbers look good. security signoff might take longer.
[08:24] Maya Chen: sounds reasonable. we'll send a benchmark spreadsheet and space to upload traces.
[08:32] [DEMO END — short break then Q/A]
[08:45] Ben Martin: small nit — we saw some mis-transcribed product names in the console export like 'Redwood Dedicated' coming out as 'Red wood dedacated' in older logs; any plan to clean that up?
[08:56] Maya Chen: we've improved transcription models; the fireflies exports sometimes mangle punctuation — totally expected.
[09:08] Aisha Patel: on VPC/private: what's the lift for on-prem? do you provide an appliance or helm charts?
[09:16] Diego Alvarez: we offer a private control-plane option with customer-managed networking; for on-prem we provide a deployable package (helm + sidecars) and ops runbook. for fully air-gapped we have an enterprise bundle with KMS/HSM options.
[09:35] Ravi Shah: any limitations on GPU types? we standardize on A100/RTX in our infra and want to avoid driver incompatibilities.
[09:43] Diego Alvarez: we certify on a set of drivers and kernels; for Dedicated we manage the instance images, for Private you'll need compatible drivers — we'll share a hardware compatibility matrix.
[09:58] Ben Martin: booking details — what does the Dedicated trial look like?
[10:04] Maya Chen: typical Dedicated POC: 2-4 week trial, we provision a small reserved pool with SLAs, run your benchmarks, and tune batching/caching. pricing depends on commit.
[10:16] Aisha Patel: for our procurement we'll need SOC2, data flow diagrams, and a DPA.
[10:22] Maya Chen: will include in the email.
[10:28] Diego Alvarez: quick note on tracing — we instrument per-token traces and console shows tail latencies and per-route breakdown so you can correlate LB timeouts to model time.
[10:40] Ben Martin: ok great. any thoughts on model quality regression if we quantize for latency?
[10:46] Diego Alvarez: quality tradeoffs exist; Redwood Optimize can run A/Bs against your eval prompts and flag regressions; quantization profiles are chosen by model/workload.
[10:58] Aisha Patel: final recap?
[11:02] Maya Chen: recap: 1) we'll send benchmark spreadsheet and security deck; 2) customer to share traces and token dist; 3) Diego to run hosted vs dedicated sim focusing on P95 and fallback behavior; 4) schedule POC scoping in first week of April.
[11:18] Ravi Shah: yep. i'll pull logs and share a sanitized sample by Friday.
[11:24] Maya Chen: perfect, thanks all. we'll follow up with calendar invite.
[11:30] Aisha Patel: thanks, bye.

(end of transcript)

Notes on transcription glitches: occasional words mis-heard (e.g., "KV cash" for KV cache, "Red wood"), timestamps approximate. This export intentionally kept conversational fillers and cross-talk to reflect a realistic meeting export.
